query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: High-throughput computational screening can be used to optimize phase stability, refine microstructures, and enhance mechanical properties by identifying alloy compositions that promote the formation of nanoscale L21 precipitates rather than extended antiphase domains.
generation.material_initial_state: A BCC matrix alloy in the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system that is predisposed to ordering into the L21 phase.
generation.intervention: Apply high-throughput computational screening to predict composition and processing conditions that favor the precipitation of nanoscale L21 particles, followed by experimental synthesis (arc-melting, homogenization, and annealing).
generation.conditions: Processing within the composition range (Al < 25 at.% and Mn > 15 at.%) using arc-melting (with multiple remelts for homogeneity), high-temperature homogenization (e.g., around 1200 °C), and subsequent annealing (e.g., at 700 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: The morphology of the ordering phase (nanoscale L21 precipitates versus ordered antiphase domains) acting as a load-bearing phase in the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Deviation from perfect L21 stoichiometry promotes the formation of nanoscale precipitates embedded in the BCC matrix, leading to enhanced load transfer and precipitation strengthening compared to continuous antiphase domains, thereby improving yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys designed via this method will exhibit refined microstructures with nanoscale L21 precipitates, which will produce higher yield strengths (e.g., enhancements on the order of hundreds of MPa) at high temperatures relative to traditional alloy systems.
generation.baseline: Traditional alloys forming BCC + continuous L21 or other ordered phases (such as D03 or B2) that do not display the refined nanoscale precipitate microstructure achieved by intentional compositional deviation.
generation.boundary: This approach is verified only for the composition window (Al < 25 at.% and Mn > 15 at.%) and under the specified processing conditions; extending the method beyond these parameters may require further validation due to limitations in thermodynamic databases.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty in the precise quantitative strengthening contribution and the long-term stability of the precipitate morphology, pending further detailed experiments and database improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti alloys with compositions both within and slightly outside the predicted optimal range. Process all samples identically (arc-melting with multiple remelts, homogenization at 1200 °C, and annealing at 700 °C). Characterize their microstructures using TEM and synchrotron XRD, and determine mechanical properties via compression tests at room and elevated temperatures.
measurements: TEM imaging to measure precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction
Synchrotron XRD for phase identification and quantification of L21 versus other phases
Compression tests to measure yield strength at temperatures up to 700 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys within the predicted optimal composition range do not exhibit the formation of nanoscale L21 precipitates and corresponding enhancements in yield strength (compared to baseline measurements of traditional BCC + ordered phase alloys), then the hypothesis that high-throughput computational screening optimizes these properties via microstructure refinement will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
